items.title: BepiColombo ends 8-year interplanetary journey to Mercury. What's next for the ambitious spacecraft?
items.summary: The BepiColombo spacecraft has overcome a last-minute computer glitch to enter orbit around Mercury — the 2nd craft in history to orbit the closest planet to the sun.
items.body: After eight years slingshotting around the inner solar system, the joint European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has finally entered into orbit around Mercury — becoming only the second mission ever to orbit the closest planet to the sun. Mission scientists confirmed on Saturday (Nov. 21) that the spacecraft reached Mercury's orbit and is transmitting data back to the ground team. However, the orbital insertion didn't go entirely as planned, European Space Agency (ESA) representatives said in a statement on Monday. Due to a software glitch, the spacecraft didn't fire its thrusters for the full 37 minutes required to slow its approach to Mercury. While ESA investigates the issue and what it means for the spacecraft's trajectory, BepiColombo remains "safe," the statement noted. The spacecraft will hopefully be ready to begin a year of intensive science observations of Mercury starting a few months from now. Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil. (Image credit: Alamy) QUICK FACTS Name: Hoxne 'Empress' pepper pot What it is: A silver spice dispenser Where it is from: Hoxne, Suffolk, England When it was made: A.D. 350 to 400 In 1992, a farmer in the village of Hoxne in southeastern England was searching for a lost hammer with a metal detector when he stumbled upon a massive hoard of more than 15,000 ancient Roman coins, jewelry and tableware. Among the artifacts in the Hoxne hoard was a silver spice container in the shape of an imperial lady. The artifact, named the Empress, is one of four pepper pots ("piperatoria" in Latin) discovered in the Hoxne hoard, according to the British Museum . The silver container stands about 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is decorated with gold around the woman's eyes, mouth, hair and accessories, including a scroll in her left hand. The woman's elaborate hairstyle helps date the creation of the pepper pot to the fourth century, but experts think the hoard may have been buried in the early fifth century, when Roman rule in Britain was ending. items.summary: Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.
items.body: A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity. This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern , a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery. Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79. In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said. The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said. During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. items.title: Why do wolves howl?
items.summary: Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.
items.body: Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl , but they are most known for their iconic howl. The eerie sound can travel vast distances and, if heard by other wolves, get them to join in with the chorus. But why do wolves howl in the first place? Experts told Live Science that the behavior is triggered not by the sight of the moon, as is commonly believed, but by the need to maintain a complex social network. Howl you doin'? Wolves can howl by themselves and in groups. "If a lone wolf howls, it's probably because they're separated from their pack and want to regain contact," Arik Kershenbaum , a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science. "Members of a pack can become quite dispersed, and when they need to hunt together, or to care for pups, or when their territory is being threatened by other wolves, they need a way of returning to each other." However, lone wolves that leave their packs may howl as well. This could be "a way of finding a new pack or mate to join," Kershenbaum said. items.body: A study of hundreds of brains has revealed molecular differences in people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) that are not found in individuals without the condition. These molecular marks also differ from those seen in the brains of people with other conditions, like depression, the research found. Our environment and experiences influence how our genes work, affecting which genes can be turned on. Rather than changing genes' underlying code, the environment can trigger what are known as epigenetic changes , which include certain chemicals that attach to DNA molecules and change their structure. One such epigenetic change, called methylation, can work like a "dimmer switch" for genes, or even completely block certain genes from turning on. "These epigenetic features of the brain are important for shaping the way the brain functions," study co-author Frances Champagne , a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, told Live Science. "This can give us some insight into why individuals with PTSD develop PTSD, or how [their brains] are different from a healthy brain." items.body: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. AI has steamrolled its way into the math community. Anthropic's proof will certainly and rightly be scrutinized, but rather than picking apart every single result these models produce, we should respond by changing how we evaluate and reward expertise — placing less weight on the volume of results and more on the human judgment required to decide which questions and answers matter. items.title: Quantum entanglement could thwart hackers and scammers, physicists reveal
items.summary: In a first-of-its-kind experiment, physicists used pairs of entangled photons to verify a person's location. That's a step toward anchoring digital security to the physical world.
items.body: For the first time, physicists have used quantum entanglement to verify a person's physical location. That could one day make it much harder for hackers to pretend to be somewhere they're not, the team says. In the new study, published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature , researchers at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) used pairs of entangled photons (particles of light) to confirm that a participant was at a specific spot between two stations on NIST's campus in Boulder, Colorado. The method is called quantum position verification, and this is the first complete demonstration of it. If the technology matures, it could help protect health records, stop remote attackers from sending commands to power grids or water treatment plants, block unauthorized stock trades and thwart phishing attacks carried out over phone or video calls, according to a statement . On Nov. 14, the Voyager mission team discovered that the nearly 50-year-old space probe had stopped sending science data back to Earth, according to NASA — a problem that the team had to deal with as recently as 2024. As of Thursday (Nov. 19), the team had not resolved the problem. But they did detect a "carrier" signal that is used to ferry science and engineering information from Voyager 1 to Earth, confirming that the probe is still powered up and pointed in the right direction. items.title: New study rewrites the role of a major speech hub in the brain
items.summary: Wernicke's area was thought to be mostly linked to understanding speech. A landmark new study has something more to say.
items.body: A new study has rewritten the role of one of the brain's major speech hubs, opening new possibilities for treating people who can't communicate verbally due to brain damage. The study, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Science , may help to solve a 150-year-old mystery in neuroscience. Nowadays, neuroscientists use cutting-edge tools to tease apart the junctions and wiring of our complex brains. But some basic theories in the field are far from new and rest on past discoveries. One of those theories concerns how the brain produces and comprehends speech. In the 1860s, German neuroanatomist Carl Wernicke identified an area of the brain that is critical to speech and usually found in the temporal lobe on the left side of the organ. Damage to Wernicke's area makes it challenging for people to understand what others are saying ‪—‬ a condition known as Wernicke's aphasia . Therefore, the brain region has been primarily thought of as a decoder that helps us break down the meaning of other people's speech. Wernicke's area (red) is found in the left temporal lobe. items.title: The immune system 'remembers' germs by tweaking its epigenetics, study shows
items.summary: A new study helps explain how the immune system's first line of defense stays ready to fight off germs and diseases.
items.body: The immune system has several ways of remembering threats it's encountered and then mounting stronger defenses in the future. Now, a new study unpacks how cells keep one type of immune memory from fading, and the findings might matter for treating diseases like cancer and Alzheimer's disease. The research zoomed in on immune cells' epigenetics ‪—‬ the methods that cells use to control genes without changing their underlying DNA codes. This can involve changing how DNA is packaged inside cells, for example. DNA molecules are typically wound around tiny spools inside cells, and their gene activity depends on how tightly or loosely they're wound. Molecules called epigenetic markers can grab hold of the spool to tweak how the DNA is wound and thus activate or silence certain genes. Past research found epigenetic changes can prime immune cells against threats. The immune system's first line of defense — innate immune cells — can be switched into an activated state so they're ready to go if they encounter a germ. items.summary: Astronomers have found two rare asteroids trailing Neptune in Vera C. Rubin Observatory data. The rocks, called Neptune's L5 Trojans, could illuminate the conditions of the infant solar system.
items.body: Astronomers using the Vera C. Rubin Observatory have discovered two ancient Trojan asteroids trailing Neptune ‪—‬ the first new ones to be spotted in 15 years. The findings, published Oct. 15 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , could improve our understanding of the early solar system while reinforcing the Rubin Observatory's potential to unearth new cosmic objects during its brisk scans of the sky. Trojan asteroids are icy, rocky bodies that dwell in a planet's vicinity but don't orbit it. Instead, these asteroids orbit the sun, following the same path as the planet. Trojan asteroids exist in distinct swarms roughly 60 degrees ahead of and behind the planet. At these points, called Lagrange points 4 and 5 (L4 and L5), respectively, the gravitational tugs of the sun and the planet balance each other, essentially "locking" the asteroids in position, according to NASA . However, very few Trojans actually hang around for billions of years. Such asteroids are likely planetary building block remnants from the solar system's infancy, and detecting them in the outer solar system can be challenging. As Pangaea broke apart, dinosaurs went on to inhabit continents all over the world, including what became Antarctica, which was a temperate rainforest during the Cretaceous period. items.title: What if space and time don't exist? Physicists are chasing hints that our reality emerges from something deeper
items.summary: Space and time seem like the bedrock of reality. But startling clues are leading physicists toward the possibility that something stranger lies beneath.
items.body: Every experience we have and every moment we live unfold naturally across space and time ‪—‬ so naturally that we rarely stop to question their existence. Physics takes this just as much for granted as we do. For more than 100 years, the field has been built upon the foundational idea that space-time — the four-dimensional fabric of the universe — is fundamental. But new insights drawn from the hearts of black holes , quantum computers and ultraprecise lasers, are now poised to challenge this assumption, leading a growing number of physicists to ask the same question: What if space and time aren't the bedrock of the universe, but emerge from something even deeper? "You can build space from a theory without space," Jeff Forshaw , a professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester in the U.K., told Live Science. Two theories that do not fit For decades, we have known that two extraordinarily successful descriptions of nature are incompatible. items.title: Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries
items.summary: On Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. Here, we look back at its most important discoveries, seen through groundbreaking space photos.
items.body: Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth. The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa. The growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe . But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us. "What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker , who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong." Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaki…

items.summary: Researchers have zeroed in on a genetic variant in the human brain that came from Neanderthals, and it might protect us from schizophrenia.
items.body: A newfound genetic variant inherited from Neanderthals may shrink a part of modern-human brains without having any meaningful effects on mental ability, and it might also reduce the risk of schizophrenia, a new study finds. "Genetic differences between Neanderthals and modern humans still influence our brains today," study co-author Hugo Zeberg , an evolutionary geneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, told Live Science. Zeberg and his colleague Svante Pääbo detailed their findings Nov. 16 in the journal PNAS . Before they went extinct around 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals were among the closest relatives of modern humans. More than a decade of research has shown that Neanderthals and modern humans once interbred. Most people not of sub-Saharan ancestry living today possess about 2% Neanderthal ancestry . Neanderthals' skulls were larger and more elongated than modern humans'. One reason for the differences has to do with the occipital lobe, the smallest of the brain's four lobes, which sits in the back of the skull. items.summary: Fossil teeth from two caves in southern China are revealing that at least two lineages of early humans were present in the region around 184,000 years ago.
items.body: Homo erectus was adaptable enough to live in rainforests in what is now southern China and may have lived alongside Denisovans there, two new studies hint. The research is based on the incredibly rare findings of nine fossil teeth from ancient humans — eight from H. erectus and one from a mystery human in the genus Homo . The teeth reveal that H. erectus lived in China much more recently than previously thought and that this population likely devoured tropical food found there. "I think it's exciting because it means that there are two hominin populations occupying these rainforest conditions there at the same time," study first author Frido Welker , a molecular palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, told Live Science. H. erectus is generally seen as the first human species to venture out of Africa, after evolving about 2 million years ago. It spread through eastern Eurasia, reaching China and Indonesia between about 1.6 million and 1.8 million years ago. It is one of the longest-surviving hominin species, and the last known record of it is from 108,000 years ago in river flood plains in Java, Indonesia . items.body: It's not often we get to peer into the tiny world of tardigrades (also known as water bears). But through his photography, biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas is unmasking the secret lives of these creatures in stunning detail. In one photo, which won Quiroga-Artigas 12th place in Nikon's 2026 Photomicrography Competition , a tardigrade ( Hypsibius exemplaris ) is seen shedding its tough outer layer, known as a cuticle or an exuvium, while laying an egg in the discarded skin. "A large part of my research involves imaging, and during the many hours I spend at the confocal microscope, I have come across some incredibly beautiful and unexpected scenes," Quiroga-Artigas, a postdoctoral researcher at the Montpellier Cell Biology Research Center in France, told Live Science in an email. "An interesting feature of tardigrade reproduction is that some species lay their eggs inside the shed cuticle, or exuvium. items.body: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack .  You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

items.body: Archaeologists have unearthed a massive 2,000-year-old tomb of an elite nomad from the Xiongnu Empire in Central Asia. The nine-level tomb contained more than 400 grave goods and is the largest Xiongnu tomb ever found in Mongolia. Archaeologists identified the enormous tomb full of riches during a four-year excavation at the site of Duurlig Nars in northern Mongolia, according to a translated statement from the National Museum of Korea, whose researchers have been excavating the site in cooperation with the Institute of Archaeology of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia. Duurlig Nars is the largest noble burial complex of the Xiongnu Empire, with nearly 300 ancient burial mounds called kurgans. The Xiongnu, also known as the Hunnu, were a collection of nomadic tribes who coalesced into a mobile empire on the Mongolian steppe in 209 B.C. The Xiongnu were connected to a broad trading network that stretched from the Roman Empire in the West to China and the Korean Peninsula in the East. items.title: For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. Now we need to fill in what we left blank.
items.summary: We need to understand how motherhood changes the brain, says neuroscientist Susana Carmona.
items.body: Look closely at the medical illustrations used in textbooks to depict the physiological changes of pregnancy, and you'll notice something strange: The bodies often have no heads. Generations of physicians learned to picture the pregnant patient as a torso — a uterus, a placenta, a growing belly — with everything above the neck left blank. That blank space is not an oversight by the illustrator. It is a faithful map of what medicine chose to study. We need to move on and create a complete picture of what happens during and after pregnancy so we can develop measures to prevent maternal deaths. For hundreds of years, we have devoted enormous effort to characterizing how pregnancy remodels nearly every organ and system in the body: the cardiovascular changes, the recalibration of the immune system, the metabolic adjustments — most of them orchestrated by hormones the placenta pours into the bloodstream. That knowledge of what is normal is exactly what lets us recognize and treat what is not, from gestational diabetes to preeclampsia. items.title: CERN physicists measure the universe at the smallest scale ever: enter the 'zeptoverse'
items.summary: Physicists at the Large Hadron Collider have detected a rare, 1-in-10-billion particle interaction that opens a view into the 'zeptoverse,' the smallest distance scale ever measured.
items.body: Using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's largest particle accelerator, scientists have gotten the first glimpse of the "zeptoverse" — the universe as it behaves within less than a hundred-trillionth of a wavelength of visible light, the smallest scale that researchers have explored to date. The new findings may one day help to answer long-standing cosmic mysteries, such as why there is far more matter than antimatter seen in the universe , and what makes up the dark matter that constitutes about 85% of all matter in the universe, the researchers announced Nov. 3 at a seminar at CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research), the organization that operates the LHC. The study, available as a preprint , has not yet been peer reviewed. At the LHC, located near Geneva at the border of France and Switzerland, researchers were investigating elusive particles called beauty quarks . These subatomic particles are cousins of the standard "up" and "down" quarks that make up the cores of all atoms in the universe. items.body: Computer models are widely used in ecological research and conservation, providing scientists with tools to predict how a given species might respond to a stressor or shift in conditions. These models can then be refined and built upon with real world data to get a better understanding of what's going on within a population and what the biggest risks are. But models aren't perfect. In this excerpt from " Start With a Bear: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet " (HarperOne, 2026), author Peter S. Alagona highlights how these models are built on the presumptions of their creators. Alagona examines the model of grizzly bear ( Ursus arctos horribilis ) habitats used by the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to inform its recovery plan for the species — and why California, despite its apparent suitability, was left out. Most of the grizzly habitat models that were introduced in the 1990s and 2000s, and then improved in the 2010s and 2020s, make two key assumptions. Although the annual Leonid meteor shower, which is famous for occasionally producing spectacular meteor storms, is active from Nov. 6 to Nov. 30, the peak on Monday into Tuesday is the best time to look, according to the American Meteor Society . Although the Leonids typically produce around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, they're among the year's fastest shooting stars, reaching 43 miles per second (70 kilometers per second), and often produce bright meteors that leave glowing trails. The best time to see them is between midnight and dawn Tuesday (Nov. 17), when the constellation Leo, from which the meteors appear to radiate, climbs higher in the eastern sky. However, shooting stars can appear anywhere in the sky. A 45%-lit waxing crescent moon will set just before midnight, leaving dark skies for meteor watching. For the best views, find a spot away from artificial lights, lie back with a wide view of the sky, and allow about 20 minutes for your eyes to become adapted to the dark. items.body: Microrobots controlled by magnets can sweep drugs towards hard-to-reach blood clots in the body, boosting the efficacy of these life-saving treatments, early tests in animals suggest. In tests with pigs, the microbots helped to dissolve clots around 10 times faster than medication alone. The research team is now working on further safety testing to ready the technology for eventual human trials. "The whole construct is inspired by nature," said lead researcher Simone Schürle , professor of medical microsystems at ETH Zürich. "There are these tiny bacteria that have little magnetic backbones which they use to navigate with the Earth's magnetic field, and we were really struck by the physics and the properties of them when exposed to rotating magnetic fields," Schürle told Live Science. ETH Zürich announced the research in a statement on Nov. 9. It has not been described in a peer-reviewed study yet. items.body: NASA's Voyager 1 probe, already the farthest human-made object in space, is about to set another record. On Nov. 18, the spacecraft will be so far from Earth that light, the universe's ultimate speed limit , takes a full 24 hours to reach it. For researchers who worked on the Voyager program and continue to study its data, the symbolic milestone of being a full light-day from Earth celebrates a mission that continues half a century after it began. Since launching in September 1977, the twin Voyager probes have outlasted many of the engineers who built them, and their flybys of the outer solar system planets remain some of the best close-up observations scientists have of those distant worlds. "Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are transcending generations," Pascal Lee , a planetary scientist at the SETI Institute who was part of the Voyager 2 team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) during its Neptune flyby in 1989, told Live Science. NASA's Voyager 1 probe , which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet. While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and " Solar System Family Portrait " images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets. One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter . From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA . items.title: How did Cleopatra really die?
items.summary: Ancient writers couldn't agree on how Egypt's last queen took her own life, and the famous snakebite story may owe more to her enemies than to the facts.
items.body: The death of Cleopatra is among the most famous in history. In 31 B.C., the Egyptian queen and her Roman ally and lover, Mark Antony, lost the Battle of Actium to Octavian, who would later become Rome's first emperor, Augustus. The following summer, Cleopatra was captured during a Roman ambush inside her royal tomb in Alexandria. According to Octavian’s account, rather than facing the disgrace of defeat, the queen allowed a venomous asp snake to bite her and quickly succumbed to its poison. Some Roman writers, such as the historian Velleius Paterculus , repeated that story without question. But others were far less certain of this account, calling it Roman propaganda to cement Octavian's rise to power. And most historians today doubt that a snake was involved at all. So how did Cleopatra die? Live Science spoke with experts, who told us that the queen's death is still shrouded in mystery. "We cannot know for sure exactly how Cleopatra died," Prudence Jones , a professor of classics at Montclair State University in New Jersey and author of "Cleopatra: A Sourcebook" (University of Oklahoma Press, 2006), told Live Science in an email. items.body: After nine days in space, the four crewmembers of NASA's Artemis II mission looked out their capsule window on April 10, 2026, and saw the bright-blue Earth below them. The crew had traveled more than 250,000 miles (400,000 kilometers) from our planet — farther from Earth than any humans had ever gone — and now, home was just a few hundred miles straight down. Only one milestone remained: splashdown , a fast and fiery plunge into the Pacific Ocean that would mark the end of humanity's first crewed mission to the moon in more than 50 years.Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen, the lone Canadian Space Agency astronaut on the crew, had every reason to be confident that the team's Orion crew capsule would hold up just fine. items.title: Which animal farts the most?
items.summary: Think that cows are the king of flatulence? There's another animal that likely blows the competition away.
items.body: Flatology, the study of flatulence , sounds more like a joke than a serious scientific discipline. But studying farts actually helps biologists understand an animal's diet and digestion. We know that a host of creatures ‪—​​ from whales, to snakes, to sloths ‪— pass gas. But do we know which animal is the top tooter? Experts told Live Science the answer is blowing in the wind. "Getting quantitative measurements for farts per animal is pretty difficult," Nick Caruso, a data scientist and co-author of '" Does It Fart?: The Definitive Field Guide to Animal Flatulence '' (Quercus Publishing, 2017), told Live Science in an email. What we can do is hypothesize using the data we do have. Expelled gas is made partially of methane, so comparing methane emissions produced by different species may provide a clue. However, this method does have limitations, experts pointed out.
